paragraphs: Choosing an algorithm involves more than knowing which methods can solve a problem. An efficient choice can depend on the structure of the particular input. This paper connects that computational problem with a psychological one: how people select a cognitive strategy when several approaches are available.

The authors treat algorithm selection as metareasoning, meaning reasoning about which reasoning procedure to use. They derive a selection method from this perspective and report that it outperforms existing methods for choosing sorting algorithms. The contribution therefore includes a concrete computational application as well as a proposed explanation of human behavior.

The same theory generates a prediction about human strategy selection, which the authors test in a behavioral experiment. Participants quickly learn to adapt their choices, and their behavior agrees with the proposed model while conflicting with the earlier theories considered. These findings make rational metareasoning a promising bridge between algorithm design and cognitive modeling; they do not establish that it explains every human strategy choice.
neurips-2014-algorithm-selection-by-rati.tldr: A metareasoning approach improves sorting-algorithm selection and matches adaptive human strategy choices in a behavioral experiment.

paragraphs: Persistent neural activity can be interpreted as a network recalling a pattern stored in its connections. Building models of this process is difficult when physiological constraints matter. Earlier proposals sometimes let individual neurons act as both excitatory and inhibitory, restrict memories to binary patterns, or produce recall with firing rates near saturation.

The paper develops a control-theoretic framework for constructing attractor networks under relevant physiological constraints. It directly optimizes networks containing excitatory and inhibitory neurons so that specified analog activity patterns become stable fixed points. In plain language, the network is designed to maintain graded patterns of activity, with stability supporting their recovery after disturbances.

The resulting networks operate in a balanced regime and withstand both corrupted memory cues and continuing noise. They also account for a reduction in variability across repeated trials after a stimulus begins, an observation associated with sensory and motor cortices. Together, these results provide a model connecting stable analog memory with physiological requirements, contributing to understanding memory mechanisms without establishing that this construction is the brain's actual implementation.
neurips-2014-analog-memories-in-a-balanc.tldr: A control-theoretic construction produces balanced excitatory–inhibitory networks that stably store analog memories and tolerate noise.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo represents an inference problem using a collection of particles. This paper introduces the particle cascade, an alternative designed to support asynchronous computation. Its central organizational change is to remove barrier synchronizations, so execution does not require all participating work to reach a shared checkpoint before proceeding.

That organization makes the method suitable for parallel and distributed implementations. The authors report improved particle throughput and memory efficiency from avoiding these barriers. The algorithm is also anytime in a specific sense: it can continue generating particles indefinitely while remaining within a fixed memory budget. Producing more particles therefore does not require retaining an ever-growing collection in memory.

The paper also proves a statistical property beyond these computational advantages: the particle cascade yields an unbiased estimator of marginal likelihood. Unbiasedness concerns the estimator's average over repeated randomness, rather than exactness of each individual estimate. This guarantee lets the estimator be inserted into existing pseudo-marginal methods, connecting a different execution strategy with established approaches to probabilistic inference.
neurips-2014-asynchronous-anytime-sequen.tldr: The particle cascade enables asynchronous, fixed-memory sequential Monte Carlo while providing an unbiased marginal-likelihood estimator.

paragraphs: Sparse signal recovery seeks a signal from linear measurements that do not uniquely determine it on their own. Sparsity supplies additional information by favoring solutions with relatively few active components. This paper considers a richer situation: there may also be prior knowledge about how those active components are arranged across the signal.

The proposed structured spike-and-slab prior encodes this arrangement through a spatial Gaussian process governing the probabilities of the spike and slab components. Rather than expressing only whether individual components are likely to be active, the model can express relationships between those probabilities. Generic covariance functions provide the mechanism for representing prior structure in the sparsity pattern.

The authors pair this prior with a Bayesian inference procedure based on expectation propagation. This makes the proposal both a modeling approach and an accompanying method for inference. Numerical experiments on synthetic data demonstrate benefits of the model. The stated evidence supports incorporating sparsity structure in this setting, with the experimental findings specifically grounded in synthetic recovery problems.
neurips-2014-bayesian-inference-for-stru.tldr: A structured spike-and-slab prior uses a spatial Gaussian process to encode sparsity patterns, with inference based on expectation propagation.

paragraphs: Interdependent-security games model voluntary investments against direct threats and risks transmitted by other agents. This paper allows full investment to reduce transmitted risk too. Depending on that reduction, agents' incentives can exhibit strategic complementarity, strategic substitutability, or both. The authors examine how these distinctions affect the difficulty of finding stable strategic outcomes.

For games combining both incentive types, deciding whether a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium exists is NP-complete. For games with complementarity alone, finding one such equilibrium takes polynomial time in the worst case. These results concern different tasks—deciding existence and constructing one equilibrium—and show that the incentive structure matters computationally.

For mixed strategies, the positive result is conditional: when each agent is indiscriminate in its transfer-risk exposure to others, all equilibria satisfying specified ordering constraints can be computed in polynomial time across the three variants. In the general transfer case, the authors establish a barrier through the NP-complete Pure-Nash-Extension problem. They also study added protection experimentally using randomly generated games with graph structures drawn from real datasets.
neurips-2014-computing-nash-equilibria-i.tldr: The difficulty of computing security-game equilibria depends on investment incentives and transfer-risk structure, with tractable special cases and general complexity barriers.

paragraphs: Atari games require an agent to interpret visual information and choose actions quickly. The paper describes a gap between strong planning-based agents and practical real-time agents. Planning methods achieve much higher scores than the best model-free approaches discussed, but run far too slowly for real-time play and use information unavailable to human players.

The proposed approach uses those slow planners to generate training data for a deep-learning architecture. Expensive planning therefore supplies examples during training, while the learned architecture handles real-time play. The title identifies offline Monte Carlo tree search as the planning approach underlying this transfer from computationally demanding decisions to a faster agent.

The authors build agents around this idea and report that they outperform DQN, their stated real-time target. The result supports using a strong but slow planner as a source of training data for a practical game-playing system. The planner's access to additional information remains part of the described setup, so the findings concern the resulting trained agents rather than a demonstration of learning under human-equivalent information conditions.
neurips-2014-deep-learning-for-real-time.tldr: Training deep networks on data from slow planning agents produces real-time Atari agents that outperform DQN in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process models diversity within a set through a positive semidefinite kernel matrix. Learning that matrix would let the model adapt its notion of diversity to a task. However, likelihood maximization over the matrix entries is nonconvex, and the learning problem is conjectured to be NP-hard.

Earlier approaches therefore concentrated on restricted convex settings, such as adjusting one weight per kernel row or mixing models with fixed kernels. This paper instead proposes learning the full kernel. It changes the representation from individual matrix entries to eigenvalues and eigenvectors, then constructs a lower bound on likelihood in the style of expectation-maximization to guide optimization.

The authors evaluate the procedure on a real-world product recommendation task. They report relative improvements of up to 16.5% in test log-likelihood over directly optimizing kernel entries with projected gradient ascent. This is evidence for more effective full-kernel fitting in the tested application; the reported metric measures probabilistic fit and does not itself establish a corresponding percentage improvement in recommendation outcomes.
neurips-2014-expectation-maximization-fo.tldr: An expectation-maximization-style procedure learns a full DPP kernel and improves test log-likelihood on a product recommendation task.

paragraphs: In online optimization, a learner repeatedly makes decisions and incurs losses as the environment unfolds. Its performance is often measured by regret: accumulated loss compared with the best single decision chosen after seeing the whole sequence. Algorithms designed for difficult worst cases can be overly cautious when the actual sequence is easier.

This paper introduces a general method that combines a safe learning algorithm with an opportunistic benchmark. The goal is to preserve useful worst-case guarantees while taking advantage of favorable data. The construction is explicitly based on having these two ingredients, rather than claiming that every existing online algorithm automatically adapts well to easier sequences.

The authors derive general regret bounds and discuss implementations across several applications, including learning with shifting experts. They also present numerical simulations for prediction with expert advice and compare against existing leading methods. The contribution is a framework for reconciling robustness with adaptability, supported by theoretical guarantees and empirical comparisons in the stated prediction setting.
neurips-2014-exploiting-easy-data-in-onl.tldr: A general online-optimization method combines a safe algorithm with an opportunistic benchmark to exploit easy data while retaining worst-case guarantees.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models with nonlinear likelihoods can require approximate inference. This paper develops two methods within a variational framework that assumes a Gaussian posterior. Both simplify the nonlinear likelihood around the current variational posterior mean, giving a common starting point for updating the approximation to the unknown quantities.

The methods differ in how they construct that simplification. One uses a Taylor expansion, while the other uses statistical linearization. The authors show that the resulting parameter updates match the state-update equations of iterative extended and unscented Kalman filters, respectively. This equivalence motivates the names extended and unscented Gaussian processes and connects the proposed inference algorithms to established filtering updates.

A practical feature of the unscented method is that it does not require derivatives of the likelihood. It can therefore treat the likelihood as a black box and applies to nondifferentiable likelihood models as well. The authors evaluate the methods on synthetic inversion problems and a binary classification dataset. The stated contribution is the inference construction and its applicability, rather than an abstract-level claim of superior performance.
neurips-2014-extended-and-unscented-gaus.tldr: Two variational GP inference methods connect to Kalman-filter updates, with the unscented version supporting derivative-free likelihood inference.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to infer class relationships between pairs of examples when only some relationships are known. The available similarity scores usually come from side information rather than class labels themselves. The task is transductive: recover relationships throughout the given collection using those similarities and a limited set of observed pairwise labels.

The algorithm has two stages. It first fills in the label submatrix associated with the labeled examples. It then reconstructs the full label matrix using that completed submatrix together with the similarity matrix. This separates completion within the partially labeled group from extending the recovered relationships to the entire collection.

The small-error recovery result depends on several conditions. The leading eigenspace of the similarity matrix must represent the label matrix's column space well, satisfy a low-coherence condition, and be accompanied by sufficiently many observed pairwise labels, along with other mild preconditions. Thus, informative similarity structure is central to the guarantee. Experiments demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness, complementing this conditional theoretical analysis.
neurips-2014-extracting-certainty-from-u.tldr: A two-stage matrix method recovers pairwise class relationships from sparse labels and similarities, with small-error guarantees under stated structural conditions.

paragraphs: This paper extends generative stochastic networks to supervised representation learning. The training objective combines a generative cost with a discriminative cost, so the model learns through both modeling data and supporting classification. A parameter called lambda sets the trade-off between these two components rather than fixing their relative influence in advance.

The authors use a noise-injection procedure called walkback training to optimize multiple network layers jointly. This makes the training process central to the approach. The reported networks do not add separate l1 or l2 regularization, dropout variants, pooling layers, or convolutional layers, allowing the authors to examine the proposed combination without those additional mechanisms.

The paper reports state-of-the-art performance on MNIST under the setup described in the abstract, along with significant improvements over baseline models on MNIST subvariants and a rectangles dataset. These findings support the effectiveness of combining generative and discriminative learning with noisy joint training. They establish performance for the evaluated settings rather than showing that the omitted architectural or regularization components are generally unnecessary.
neurips-2014-general-stochastic-networks.tldr: Hybrid generative–discriminative training with injected noise gives stochastic networks strong classification results without added convolution, pooling, or standard regularizers.

paragraphs: An exploring agent can choose actions for the information they provide about an unfamiliar environment. Earlier work showed that this principle can efficiently build models of probabilistic environments with discrete, bounded state spaces. The paper addresses a harder setting in which the space of possible states is unbounded.

The authors use nonparametric Bayesian models to support information-based learning in that setting. Their specific model is the Chinese Restaurant Process. Its role is to provide a way of modeling an environment without requiring a fixed finite collection of possible states, making it relevant when exploration can keep revealing previously unrepresented possibilities.

The paper demonstrates that the Chinese Restaurant Process model can address this learning problem. It further shows that an Empirical Bayes version explores both bounded and unbounded worlds efficiently while relying on little prior information. The findings extend the demonstrated reach of information-driven exploration beyond bounded environments. They support this particular modeling approach rather than establishing that any information-seeking agent will explore an arbitrary unbounded world efficiently.
neurips-2014-information-based-learning-.tldr: A Chinese Restaurant Process model enables information-driven exploration of unbounded state spaces, with an Empirical Bayes version requiring little prior information.

paragraphs: Estimating human pose from a single image requires locating body joints while accounting for how those joints fit together. The paper addresses this articulated pose-estimation problem with a hybrid architecture. It combines a deep convolutional network with a Markov random field, bringing two modeling approaches into the same system.

The architecture can exploit structural knowledge about the task, including geometric relationships between joint locations. These relationships provide information beyond the appearance of an isolated location in the image. The graphical component offers a way to incorporate that structure alongside the convolutional network, so pose estimation can use visual evidence together with constraints on relationships between body parts.

The authors show that training the two components jointly improves performance and allows their system to significantly outperform the existing state-of-the-art techniques considered. The central finding is therefore about learning the combined architecture, as well as choosing its components. It supports coordinating visual representation learning with structured pose modeling for the monocular image task evaluated in the paper.
neurips-2014-joint-training-of-a-convolu.tldr: Jointly training a convolutional network and a Markov random field improves single-image human pose estimation by incorporating structural relationships.

paragraphs: A pseudo-ensemble is a collection of models created by randomly perturbing one parent model. The collection may even be infinite. Dropout provides an example: randomly masking nodes creates different child subnetworks. The paper uses this perspective to study variation in the model itself, alongside ensemble learning and robustness approaches that perturb observations.

The authors introduce a regularizer that encourages the pseudo-ensemble's behavior to remain robust to the noise used to generate its members. The organizing idea is consistency under model perturbations. This provides a training principle that can be applied to a family of child models instead of treating their random differences only as a training device.

In fully supervised learning, the regularizer matches dropout's performance. It also extends naturally to semi-supervised learning, where the authors report state-of-the-art results. A separate sentiment-analysis case study converts a Recursive Neural Tensor Network into a pseudo-ensemble and significantly improves its benchmark performance. These findings show the framework's usefulness across the stated learning settings and one concrete model transformation.
neurips-2014-learning-with-pseudo-ensemb.tldr: Regularizing consistency among randomly perturbed child models matches dropout in supervised learning and delivers strong semi-supervised and sentiment-analysis results.

paragraphs: A multiclass object detector must reject non-targets and distinguish among target categories. This paper organizes those decisions into a cascade with progressively finer class distinctions. Early stages make binary target-versus-non-target decisions, later stages separate target classes in detail, and intermediate stages use numbers of classes learned from data.

The authors create this structure through structurally biased boosting, or SBBoost. Their analysis identifies two complementary tendencies in earlier multiclass boosting methods: emphasizing difficult examples and emphasizing difficult classes. SBBoost generalizes the class-based tendency so that learning can favor the desired cascade structure, using a multiclass margin with adjustable bias parameters.

A stage-adaptive policy chooses those parameters from data. The algorithm can also be understood through margin thresholds or as cost-sensitive boosting, giving several views of the same structural control. The resulting cascades combine high detection rates with computational efficiency, and experiments report improvements over earlier solutions. The practical idea is to reserve fine distinctions for later stages while using simpler decisions to eliminate false positives early.
neurips-2014-multi-resolution-cascades-f.tldr: Structurally biased boosting learns efficient object-detection cascades that progress from binary rejection to fine multiclass discrimination.

paragraphs: An agent acting in the world must choose actions from observations that are noisy and incomplete. Optimal control describes this problem through a cost function and a rule for selecting actions from observations. Standard formulations usually treat the sensors as fixed, leaving the action-selection rule as the object to optimize.

This paper considers the additional flexibility available when sensory encoding can also adapt. For biological systems, the purpose of that adaptation may be to improve control rather than perception alone. The authors show that these two objectives lead to different sensory adaptations, and that the distinction already arises in simple control settings.

The result means that a sensory representation should be assessed in relation to the task it supports. Improving perception and improving action selection cannot simply be assumed to call for the same adaptation. The authors connect this conclusion with recent experimental findings, which they describe as consistent with their analysis. Their contribution is a control-theoretic reason to include behavioral objectives when studying changes in sensory coding.
neurips-2014-optimal-neural-codes-for-co.tldr: Sensory adaptation optimized for control can differ from adaptation optimized for perception, making the agent's task essential to understanding neural coding.

paragraphs: Regularization controls model complexity by restricting or penalizing its parameters. This paper proposes a framework based on transformations of parameter space. A mathematical group acts on the parameters, and a selected orbit collects the points reached through those transformations. The allowed parameter region is the convex hull of that orbit, called an orbitope.

This construction places several familiar regularizers within a shared geometric framework. The authors also connect the sorted 1-norm with the hyperoctahedral group. These relationships matter because they explain apparently separate regularization choices through the group structure used to generate their feasible regions, rather than treating each penalty as an unrelated construction.

The paper then addresses computation by deriving properties that make a group suitable for conditional-gradient and projected-gradient optimization. It also proposes a continuation strategy for exploring orbits and presents simulations involving symmetric and hyperoctahedral groups. The contribution combines a unifying description of regularization with conditions for practical optimization; it does not assert that every group yields an equally tractable learning problem.
neurips-2014-orbit-regularization-c81310.tldr: Orbit regularization unifies complexity constraints through group-generated convex regions and identifies conditions for gradient-based optimization.

paragraphs: Discovering a causal graph can require controlled experiments to resolve relationships left ambiguous by existing information. This paper asks how many experiments are needed when the designer can randomize their selection. The distinction matters because the earlier lower bounds discussed in the paper assume that experiment selection cannot use randomization.

In an adversarial setting, the authors show that randomized design can recover the graph using at most O(log log n) experiments in expectation. They also show that this rate is tight for some causal graphs. The expectation qualification is essential: the result bounds the average over randomness, rather than promising that every execution uses that many experiments.

Under a different assumption, where the graph is drawn uniformly under an Erdős–Rényi model, the expected experiment count becomes constant. The analysis uses structural properties of essential graphs and operations that force edge orientations. It also identifies different roles for these operations in worst-case and average-case settings. Computer simulations complement the theoretical results, whose improvements depend on the stated randomization and graph-generation settings.
neurips-2014-randomized-experimental-des.tldr: Randomized experiment selection reduces expected causal-discovery experiment counts, with tight worst-case bounds and constant expectations under an Erdős–Rényi model.

paragraphs: Human choices exhibit recurring patterns that a choice model should be able to represent. This paper focuses on three such phenomena: similarity, attraction, and compromise effects. The authors extend the multinomial logit model to accommodate these patterns, making the representation of observed choice behavior the central modeling objective.

The work includes a formal analysis of how strongly the extended model can express each phenomenon. This goes beyond showing a few illustrative choices: it quantifies aspects of the model's flexibility. The authors then show that the choice model has a restricted Boltzmann machine representation and that its parameters can be learned effectively from data.

Numerical experiments use real human-choice data. The results suggest that training can produce a model exhibiting the characteristic choice phenomena considered in the paper. That empirical conclusion is appropriately narrower than claiming a complete account of human decisions. The contribution links a behavioral choice formulation, a formal description of its expressive capacity, and a learnable probabilistic model in one framework.
neurips-2014-restricted-boltzmann-machin.tldr: An extended multinomial logit model represents characteristic human-choice effects and can be learned through a restricted Boltzmann machine formulation.

paragraphs: Self-paced learning gradually introduces training examples from easier to more complex ones. This paper argues that difficulty alone leaves out an important consideration: diversity among the selected examples. The proposed method, self-paced learning with diversity, explicitly favors examples that are both easy and diverse as training proceeds.

The authors express these preferences through a general regularization term. Because that term is independent of the learning objective, the approach can be adapted to different learning tasks. Although the sample-selection optimization is nonconvex, the variables in this regularizer can be optimized globally in linearithmic time. That guarantee concerns the selection subproblem, rather than global optimization of every model trained with it.

Experiments on three real-world datasets show significant improvements over conventional self-paced learning. On Hollywood2 and Olympic Sports, the method achieves the highest mean average precision reported in the literature considered by the paper. The findings support treating diversity as an explicit part of a training curriculum, alongside example difficulty, with both an efficient selection procedure and empirical evidence in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2014-self-paced-learning-with-di.tldr: Adding diversity to self-paced sample selection improves reported results while allowing globally optimal, efficient optimization of the selection regularizer.

paragraphs: Multiple senses can provide overlapping information about the same underlying stimulus. One proposed standard for successful integration is that multisensory neurons preserve all stimulus information available in their separate sensory inputs. This is a stronger perspective than judging integration only by how much it reduces estimation error.

Earlier empirical work found that a network trained for latent-variable density estimation met this information-preservation criterion. Its observed data were the activities of unisensory neurons, and its architecture was not designed to reproduce the true data-generating process. That result raised a theoretical question: why should learning a probability distribution also produce the desired form of sensory integration?

This paper proves an analytical connection for the model used in that earlier work. In that setting, density estimation implies sensory integration under the information-preservation criterion. The authors also state that the implication does not appear to hold for all models. The finding therefore explains a specific empirical result and establishes a model-dependent connection, rather than a universal equivalence between density learning and optimal sensory integration.
neurips-2014-sensory-integration-and-den.tldr: The paper proves that density estimation implies information-preserving sensory integration for a particular model, while cautioning against universalizing the connection.

paragraphs: The k-support norm was developed for prediction problems involving sparse vectors. This paper places it within a larger family called box-norms. That broader perspective provides both a way to study related regularizers together and a route to improving the computation required to use them in optimization.

Within this framework, the authors derive an efficient proximity-operator algorithm for the squared norm, improving on the original k-support method. Such an operator handles the regularization part of an optimization update. They also move from vectors to matrices by introducing the spectral k-support norm and establish a close relationship with the multitask learning cluster norm.

The matrix norms are evaluated on real and synthetic matrix-completion datasets, where the task is to recover missing matrix entries. The reported findings indicate state-of-the-art performance for spectral k-support regularization, with consistent improvements over trace-norm regularization and the matrix elastic net in those experiments. The contribution thus combines a broader mathematical framework, improved optimization machinery, and empirical support for the matrix extension.
neurips-2014-spectral-k-support-norm-reg.tldr: The paper generalizes k-support regularization to matrices, improves a key optimization step, and reports strong matrix-completion performance.

paragraphs: Ambiguous prediction tasks can benefit from several strong, diverse candidate answers. In structured problems, however, each answer may be an entire image labeling or sentence parse, making the possible candidate set exponentially large. Searching directly through that space to assemble a useful collection is therefore a substantial computational challenge.

This paper studies greedy selection by connecting submodular diversity functions with high-order potentials in graphical models. The key condition is that the marginal gain from adding a candidate admits a structured representation. When that condition holds, the next greedy addition can be sought through inference in a factor graph equipped with appropriately constructed high-order potentials.

The authors show through examples that these representations enable approximate maximization in time sublinear in the size of the candidate space. They discuss benefits and trade-offs and report substantially better proposals from their constructions. The result is conditional on exploitable structure in the marginal gains: it supplies a way to use graphical-model inference for diverse candidate selection without claiming efficient optimization for every possible diversity function.
neurips-2014-submodular-meets-structured.tldr: Structured marginal gains let greedy diversity selection use factor-graph inference to search enormous candidate spaces approximately and efficiently.

paragraphs: Private maximization asks an algorithm to choose an item with a high data-dependent score while satisfying differential privacy. Because this selection problem appears inside many statistical and machine-learning procedures, improvements to it can matter beyond a single application. The challenge is to preserve selection quality while respecting the privacy constraint.

The paper identifies a limitation of previous approaches: their utility either deteriorates as the universe of possible items grows, or their applicability is confined to restricted function classes. It introduces what the authors describe as the first general-purpose, range-independent algorithm for this problem. Here, range independence addresses the dependence of utility on the size of the item universe.

The privacy guarantee is approximate differential privacy, a qualification that is part of the stated result. The authors demonstrate applicability to two fundamental tasks in data mining and machine learning. The main contribution is therefore a broadly applicable private-selection mechanism whose utility avoids the identified universe-size dependence, rather than a claim that privacy has no cost or that computation is independent of universe size.
neurips-2014-the-large-margin-mechanism-.tldr: A general-purpose private-maximization algorithm avoids utility dependence on the item-universe size while guaranteeing approximate differential privacy.

paragraphs: State-space models describe systems whose underlying state evolves over time and is observed indirectly. This paper develops efficient Bayesian learning for nonlinear versions using sparse Gaussian processes. The learning output is a tractable posterior over nonlinear dynamical systems, retaining uncertainty about the dynamics rather than producing only a single fitted description.

The approach offers a way to trade model capacity against computational cost while avoiding overfitting, as described by the authors. This is presented as an advantage relative to conventional parametric models. Sparse Gaussian processes provide the modeling basis, while variational Bayesian learning makes the posterior manageable for the proposed inference procedure.

The main algorithm combines variational Bayes with sequential Monte Carlo in a hybrid inference approach. The paper also presents stochastic variational inference and online-learning versions aimed at fast learning from long time series. Together, these contributions address both flexibility in representing nonlinear dynamics and the practical burden of learning them. The emphasis is on a usable uncertainty-aware model and adaptable computation, including approaches intended for longer streams of observations.
neurips-2014-variational-gaussian-proces.tldr: Sparse Gaussian processes and hybrid variational inference provide tractable Bayesian learning of nonlinear dynamics, with extensions for long time series.
